criterion_notes.c1: Topically addresses drinking water delivery and provisioning for urban and rural communities and households in Cameroon alongside broader national water resources management.
criterion_notes.c2: PASSES plain wording, FAILS narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the paper examines legal, administrative, institutional, and governance factors by chronically reviewing Cameroon's water legislation, decrees, ministries, and administrative structures from pre-colonial times to 2010. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, however, it fails because it treats unanalysed macro-governance background, general water-resource statutes, ministerial organograms/overlaps, and secondary accounts of community self-help project delivery (Njoh 2002, 2006) rather than analyzing a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (brief descriptive mentions of colonial water rates, SNEC bill arrears/interruptions, and the CAMWATER/CDE public-private split are historical background only). Note that plain_criterion2_decision is still exclude because the paper independently fails c3, c4, and c5 (E05).
criterion_notes.c3: Historical-institutional narrative and doctrinal/policy overview rather than an empirical study or systematic empirical synthesis (E05). Although the authors state they used 'personal observations' and archival/parliamentary records, there is no empirical methodology, sampling, qualitative protocol, or systematic data analysis; the paper catalogues statutes and decrees, presents conceptual organograms, summarizes two published project cases from Njoh (2002, 2006), and reports a two-row archival table of 1999 municipal council arrears owed to SNEC.
criterion_notes.c4: Does not measure or empirically report a household- or community-level water or sanitation service access outcome (connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion). Table 2 reports unpaid utility debt of two municipal councils to SNEC in 1999, Table 1 reproduces Njoh's (2002, 2006) project determinants, and statements about domestic water shortages, vendor prices, or household wells in Douala are unmeasured background or anecdotal assertions.
criterion_notes.c5: Lacks an identifiable empirical study design, study population/sample, and evaluable exposure-to-access-outcome relationship; unit of discussion is the national historical water-governance system of Cameroon from pre-1900 to 2010.

study_design: Historical-institutional and doctrinal policy overview / narrative review (non-empirical)
population_and_sample: not reported (macro-historical discussion of Cameroon's national water management institutions, citing secondary cases of Mutengene and Kumbo communities and 1999 SNEC debts of Buea Rural and Limbe Urban Councils)
exposure: Historical evolution of national water legislation, administrative decrees, and institutional management structures in Cameroon (pre-1900 to 2010)
outcome: not reported (no empirically measured household or community service access outcome; narrative assertions of poor water provisioning, secondary project summaries from Njoh 2002/2006, and 1999 municipal council bad debts to SNEC)
rationale: Exclude as E05 (No empirical evidence). Oumar and Tewari (2012) present a historical, doctrinal, and macro-institutional policy overview of water management frameworks and administrative structures in Cameroon from pre-colonial times to 2010. Although the text claims 'personal observations' alongside parliamentary and archival records, it contains no identifiable empirical research design, sampling, or primary empirical measurement of household or community water access outcomes—consisting instead of chronological summaries of statutes and decrees, institutional organograms, secondary summaries of two community water projects from Njoh (2002, 2006), a two-council table of 1999 SNEC debt arrears, and normative policy recommendations. Additionally, while the paper satisfies the plain wording of Criterion 2 by reviewing water laws and institutions, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because it addresses macro-governance background and ministerial structures rather than empirically analyzing a rule-type mechanism governing service access; under both readings of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for lack of empirical access evidence (c3, c4, c5).
